header:
Inflation came back
What it means for you

lines.text: Pay rose 3%. Prices rose 3.7%.
lines.say: Pay rose three percent. Prices rose three point seven.

lines.text: So after a year of raises, real hourly pay is down 0.7% (BLS, Sept 2026).
lines.say: So after a whole year of raises, real hourly pay for the average worker is down zero point seven percent, the Labor Department says.

lines.text: That's not a typo. Prices simply ran faster than pay.
lines.say: That's not a typo. Prices simply ran faster than pay.

lines.text: And that was only one of the inflation reports out on Oct 14 and 15, 2026.
lines.say: And that was only one of the inflation reports that landed on October fourteenth and fifteenth.

lines.text: Consumer prices: up 3.7% in a year. Producer prices: up 6.3%.
lines.say: Consumer prices, up three point seven percent in a year. Producer prices, up six point three percent.

lines.text: Mortgage rates: 7.4%. And a 3.6% raise for Social Security.
lines.say: Mortgage rates, seven point four percent. And a three point six percent raise for Social Security.

lines.text: The Fed already raised rates in Sept 2026, to 3.75-4.00%.
lines.say: The Federal Reserve already raised rates in September, to a range of three point seven five to four percent.

lines.text: And it decides again on Oct 28.
lines.say: And it decides again on October twenty-eighth.

lines.text: So is this the 1970s again? Or 2022? Not exactly, and the difference matters.
lines.say: So is this the nineteen seventies all over again? Or twenty twenty-two? Not exactly, and the difference matters.

lines.text: Coming up: what happened, pay vs prices, lessons from the 1970s, and your money.
lines.say: Coming up: what happened, pay versus prices, lessons from the seventies, and what it means for your money.

lines.text: Chapter 1: What happened
lines.say: Let's start with what happened.

lines.text: Here's inflation in 2026, month by month: prices vs a year earlier (BLS).
lines.say: Here's inflation in twenty twenty-six, month by month. Each point compares prices with a year earlier.

lines.text: It was 2.4% in Jan and Feb, then jumped after the Iran war began in late Feb and energy prices surged.
lines.say: It sat at two point four percent in January and February, then jumped after the Iran war began in late February and energy prices surged.

lines.text: It peaked at 4.2% in May, cooled to 3.4% over the summer, then rose to 3.7% in Sept.
lines.say: It peaked at four point two percent in May, cooled to three point four over the summer, and climbed back to three point seven in September.

lines.text: The main culprit: gasoline, up 9.1% in Sept alone.
lines.say: The main culprit was gasoline, which rose nine point one percent in September alone.

lines.text: Gas made up more than half of Sept's increase, and it's up about 34% from a year earlier.
lines.say: Gas made up more than half of September's increase, and it's up about thirty-four percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: Strip out food and energy, and 'core' inflation is 2.6%, not 3.7%.
lines.say: Strip out food and energy, and what economists call core inflation is two point six percent, not three point seven.

lines.text: Groceries dipped 0.1% in Sept. Food at home is up 1.8% in a year.
lines.say: Groceries actually dipped point one percent in September, and food at home is up just one point eight percent in a year.

lines.text: Shoppers felt the gas part: Sept retail sales at gas stations rose 6.4% (Census).
lines.say: Shoppers felt the gas part. In September, sales at gas stations jumped six point four percent, the Census Bureau reported.

lines.text: Then on Oct 15, producer prices jumped 1.3% in one month.
lines.say: Then, on October fifteenth, the producer price index, which tracks what businesses get paid, jumped one point three percent in a single month.

lines.text: That's the biggest monthly jump since March 2022.
lines.say: That's the biggest monthly jump since March twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: Over a year: producer prices are up 6.3%, the most since Dec 2022.
lines.say: Over twelve months, producer prices are up six point three percent, the most since December twenty twenty-two.

lines.text: Producer prices are costs upstream. Businesses either pass them on or absorb them.
lines.say: Why does that matter? Producer prices are costs upstream. Businesses either pass them on to shoppers or absorb them in their profits.

lines.text: Mortgage rates: Freddie Mac's 30-year average held at 7.4% on Oct 15, the highest since Nov 2023.
lines.say: Mortgage rates are up too. Freddie Mac's average thirty-year rate held at seven point four percent on October fifteenth, the highest since November twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: In late Feb 2026, it was 5.98%.
lines.say: Back in late February, it was five point nine eight percent.

lines.text: Example: on a $300,000 loan, that's about $1,795 a month vs $2,077 (principal and interest only).
lines.say: In a made-up example, on a three hundred thousand dollar loan, that's about seventeen hundred ninety-five dollars a month versus two thousand seventy-seven, for principal and interest.

lines.text: That's about $282 more every month for the same loan.
lines.say: That's about two hundred eighty-two dollars more every month, for the very same loan.

lines.text: Chapter 2: Pay vs prices
lines.say: Now, the number a lot of people missed: what happened to paychecks.

lines.text: Average hourly pay rose 3% in the year to Sept, to $37.81 an hour (BLS).
lines.say: Average hourly pay rose three percent in the year to September, to thirty-seven dollars and eighty-one cents an hour.

lines.text: Prices rose 3.7%. So prices won the race.
lines.say: Prices rose three point seven percent. So prices won the race.

lines.text: Economists call this 'real' pay: roughly your raise minus inflation.
lines.say: Economists call this real pay. It's roughly your raise minus inflation. Three minus three point seven is minus zero point seven.

lines.text: In Sept alone, pay rose 0.1% while prices rose 0.6%.
lines.say: And in September alone, pay rose zero point one percent, while prices rose zero point six.

lines.text: Example: a $50,000 salary with a 3% raise becomes $51,500.
lines.say: Here's a made-up example. A fifty thousand dollar salary with a three percent raise becomes fifty-one thousand five hundred.

lines.text: To keep pace with 3.7% prices, it would need to be $51,850. That's $350 short.
lines.say: To keep pace with prices up three point seven percent, it would need to be fifty-one thousand eight hundred fifty. That's three hundred fifty dollars short.

lines.text: Longer hours softened it: real weekly pay fell only 0.1%, as the average workweek got longer.
lines.say: Longer hours softened the hit. Real weekly pay fell only zero point one percent, because the average workweek got longer.

lines.text: Hiring also slowed: employers added just 29,000 jobs in Sept, and unemployment was 4.2%.
lines.say: Hiring has slowed, too. Employers added just twenty-nine thousand jobs in September, and unemployment was four point two percent.

lines.text: Slower hiring usually means less pressure for bigger raises.
lines.say: Slow hiring usually means less pressure on employers to hand out bigger raises.

lines.text: Retirees get a raise: Social Security's 2027 COLA is 3.6% (SSA, Oct 14).
lines.say: Retirees are getting a raise. On October fourteenth, Social Security announced a three point six percent cost-of-living increase for twenty twenty-seven.

lines.text: It's the largest since 2023's 8.7%. The 2026 raise was 2.8%.
lines.say: It's the largest since twenty twenty-three, when it was eight point seven percent. The twenty twenty-six raise was two point eight.

lines.text: Example: on a $2,000 monthly check, 3.6% adds $72, to $2,072.
lines.say: In a made-up example, on a two thousand dollar monthly check, three point six percent adds seventy-two dollars, to two thousand seventy-two.

lines.text: About 72 million people get it starting in Jan 2027.
lines.say: Nearly seventy-two million Social Security beneficiaries get it starting in January.

lines.text: The COLA tracks a version of CPI, so it's built to keep up with prices, not beat them.
lines.say: The raise is tied to a version of the consumer price index, so it's built to keep up with prices, not get ahead of them.

lines.text: Chapter 3: We've seen this before
lines.say: To see why everyone's watching the Fed, let's go back about fifty years.

lines.text: Here's US inflation by year from 1972 (annual average, BLS).
lines.say: Here's US inflation by year, starting in nineteen seventy-two, when it was three point two percent.

lines.text: Oil shocks in 1973 and 1979 helped push it to 11% in 1974 and 13.5% in 1980.
lines.say: Oil shocks in nineteen seventy-three and nineteen seventy-nine helped push it to eleven percent in nineteen seventy-four, and thirteen point five percent in nineteen eighty.

lines.text: In between, it never fell back to where it started, so price rises kept stacking up.
lines.say: In between, it never fell back to where it started, so price rises kept stacking up.

lines.text: Measured month by month, the 12-month rate peaked at 14.8% in March 1980.
lines.say: Measured month by month, the yearly rate peaked at fourteen point eight percent in March nineteen eighty.

lines.text: In Oct 1979, new Fed Chair Paul Volcker announced a tough anti-inflation plan.
lines.say: In October nineteen seventy-nine, the new Fed chair, Paul Volcker, announced a tough plan to break inflation.

lines.text: The Fed's key rate hit a record 20% in late 1980.
lines.say: The Fed's key interest rate hit a record twenty percent in late nineteen eighty.

lines.text: Mortgage rates hit 18.63% in Oct 1981 (Freddie Mac).
lines.say: Thirty-year mortgage rates reached eighteen point six three percent in October nineteen eighty-one.

lines.text: It worked, at a cost: unemployment peaked at 10.8% in late 1982.
lines.say: It worked, but at a painful cost. Unemployment peaked at ten point eight percent in late nineteen eighty-two.

lines.text: By 1983, inflation was back to 3.2%.
lines.say: By nineteen eighty-three, inflation was back down to three point two percent.

lines.text: The lesson the Fed took: inflation that lingers gets harder to stop.
lines.say: The lesson central bankers took from the seventies: inflation that lingers gets much harder to stop.

lines.text: Fast-forward: in Jan 2021, mortgages hit a record low 2.65%. In March 2022, the Fed started hiking from near zero.
lines.say: Now fast-forward. In January twenty twenty-one, mortgage rates hit a record low of two point six five percent. In March twenty twenty-two, the Fed started hiking from near zero.

lines.text: Inflation hit 9.1% in June 2022, the most since 1981.
lines.say: Inflation hit nine point one percent in June twenty twenty-two, the most since nineteen eighty-one.

lines.text: By July 2023, after 11 hikes, the Fed's range was 5.25-5.5%.
lines.say: By July twenty twenty-three, after eleven hikes, the Fed's range was five point two five to five point five percent.

lines.text: 2022 was rough for 401(k)s: the S&P 500 fell 19.4% and the Nasdaq 33.1%.
lines.say: Twenty twenty-two was rough for four oh one Ks. The S and P five hundred fell nineteen point four percent, and the Nasdaq thirty-three point one.

lines.text: Bonds didn't help: the main US bond index fell more than 12% in 2022, its worst year on record.
lines.say: Bonds didn't help either. The main US bond index fell more than twelve percent in twenty twenty-two, its worst year on record.

lines.text: When rates rise, existing bond prices fall, and stocks often wobble too.
lines.say: That's because when rates rise, the prices of existing bonds fall, and stocks often wobble too.

lines.text: So is 2026 a replay? Core inflation was 5.9% in June 2022. In Sept 2026, it's 2.6%.
lines.say: So is twenty twenty-six a replay? Not quite. Core inflation was five point nine percent in June twenty twenty-two. In September twenty twenty-six, it's two point six.

lines.text: 2026's jump is mostly energy, a bit like the 1970s oil shocks. The question is whether it spreads.
lines.say: This jump is mostly about energy, a bit like the oil shocks of the seventies. The big question is whether it spreads into everything else.

lines.text: One detail most people miss: the Fed's 3.75-4% range is barely above 3.7% inflation.
lines.say: And here's a detail most people miss. The Fed's target range, three point seven five to four percent, is barely above inflation at three point seven.

lines.text: Rate minus inflation is the 'real' interest rate. Now it's about 0%. In 1981 it was far above zero.
lines.say: Rate minus inflation is called the real interest rate. Right now, it's close to zero. In nineteen eighty-one, it was far above zero.

lines.text: Chapter 4: Savings, debt and 401(k)
lines.say: So what does all of this mean for your own money?

lines.text: The average US savings account paid 0.38% in July 2026 (FDIC national rate).
lines.say: Start with savings. The national average savings account rate was zero point three eight percent in July, according to the F D I C.

lines.text: Example: $10,000 at 0.38% earns $38 in a year.
lines.say: In a made-up example, ten thousand dollars at that rate earns thirty-eight dollars in a year.

lines.text: But with prices up 3.7%, the same stuff costs $370 more.
lines.say: But with prices up three point seven percent, the same stuff now costs three hundred seventy dollars more.

lines.text: So in real terms, that cash lost buying power.
lines.say: So in real terms, that cash lost buying power.

lines.text: Some online savings accounts and Treasury bills pay closer to the Fed's rate. Example: at 4%, $10,000 earns $400.
lines.say: Some online savings accounts and Treasury bills pay closer to the Fed's rate. At an example rate of four percent, the same ten thousand dollars earns four hundred.

lines.text: A math trick, the rule of 72: 72 divided by 3.7 is about 19.5.
lines.say: Here's a math trick called the rule of seventy-two. Seventy-two divided by three point seven is about nineteen point five.

lines.text: That's about how many years prices take to double at 3.7% a year. Math, not a forecast.
lines.say: That's about how many years prices would take to double at that pace. It's math, not a forecast.

lines.text: Debt: card accounts charged interest averaged 22.15% APR in Q2 2026 (Fed).
lines.say: Now debt. Credit card accounts that were charged interest averaged a twenty-two point one five percent A P R in the second quarter, Fed data show.

lines.text: Example: a $5,000 balance at 22.15% costs about $1,108 a year in interest.
lines.say: In a made-up example, a five thousand dollar balance at that rate costs about eleven hundred eight dollars a year in interest.

lines.text: Most card rates float with the prime rate, now 7%. The Sept hike added about $12.50 a year on that balance.
lines.say: Most card rates float with the prime rate, now seven percent. September's quarter-point hike adds about twelve dollars and fifty cents a year on that balance.

lines.text: Fixed-rate debt is different: a fixed mortgage or car payment stays the same as prices rise.
lines.say: Fixed-rate debt works differently. A fixed mortgage or car payment stays the same, even as prices and paychecks rise around it.

lines.text: Variable-rate debt, like cards and home equity lines, can get pricier when the Fed hikes.
lines.say: Variable-rate debt, like credit cards and home equity lines, can get pricier when the Fed hikes.

lines.text: Your 401(k): stocks have held up so far. The S&P 500 set a record close of about 7,819 on Oct 6, 2026.
lines.say: And your four oh one K? Stocks have held up so far. The S and P five hundred closed at a record of about seven thousand eight hundred nineteen on October sixth.

lines.text: But the 10-year Treasury yield topped 5.3% in early Oct, its highest since 2002.
lines.say: But the ten-year Treasury yield climbed above five point three percent in early October, its highest since two thousand two.

lines.text: Higher yields mean new bonds pay more, but bonds already in your fund are worth less.
lines.say: Higher yields mean new bonds pay more, but bonds already sitting in your fund are worth less.

lines.text: 2022 showed stocks and bonds can fall at the same time. That's history, not a forecast.
lines.say: Twenty twenty-two showed that stocks and bonds can fall at the same time. That's history, not a forecast.

lines.text: Chapter 5: Winners, losers, what's next
lines.say: So who comes out ahead, and who falls behind?

lines.text: Ahead: higher-rate savers, people with low fixed-rate loans, and banks.
lines.say: Ahead: savers earning higher rates, people with low fixed-rate loans locked in, and banks.

lines.text: Behind: workers whose raises trail prices, home buyers, and card borrowers.
lines.say: Behind: workers whose raises trail prices, home buyers, and anyone carrying a card balance.

lines.text: Banks, for example: Bank of America's net interest income rose 8% to $16.4B in Q3 2026.
lines.say: Take banks. Bank of America's net interest income rose eight percent, to sixteen point four billion dollars, in the third quarter.

lines.text: At JPMorgan, card borrowers are mostly keeping up: its card charge-off rate fell to 2.91% in Q3, from 3.15% a year earlier.
lines.say: So far, card borrowers at JPMorgan are mostly keeping up. Its card charge-off rate fell to two point nine one percent in the third quarter, from three point one five a year earlier.

lines.text: Renters feel it too: shelter costs are up 3.2% in a year.
lines.say: Renters feel it too. Shelter costs are up three point two percent from a year earlier.

lines.text: Dates to watch: Oct 22, mortgage rates. Oct 28, the Fed's decision.
lines.say: Now, the dates to watch. On October twenty-second, Freddie Mac posts new mortgage rates. On October twenty-eighth, the Fed announces its decision.

lines.text: Nov 10: October inflation and real pay. Nov 13: producer prices.
lines.say: On November tenth, the October inflation report and the real pay numbers arrive together. And on November thirteenth, producer prices.

lines.text: In each, watch gas prices, core inflation, real pay and how the Fed describes inflation.
lines.say: In each one, watch the same four things: gas prices, core inflation, real pay, and how the Fed describes inflation.

lines.text: In Sept, the Fed put it in three words.
lines.say: In September, the Fed's statement put it in three words: inflation remains elevated.

lines.text: Chapter 6: Recap
lines.say: Let's recap.

lines.text: Consumer prices are up 3.7% in a year, mostly because of gas. Core is 2.6%.
lines.say: Consumer prices are up three point seven percent in a year, mostly because of gas. Core inflation is two point six.

lines.text: Average pay is up 3%, so real hourly pay is down 0.7%.
lines.say: Average pay is up three percent, so real hourly pay is down zero point seven.

lines.text: Mortgage rates are 7.4%, the highest since Nov 2023.
lines.say: Mortgage rates are at seven point four percent, the highest since November twenty twenty-three.

lines.text: And the Fed decides on Oct 28, with its rate barely above inflation.
lines.say: And the Fed decides on October twenty-eighth, with its rate barely above inflation.

lines.text: It's not the 1970s, and it's not 2022. But prices are outrunning paychecks again.
lines.say: It's not the seventies, and it's not twenty twenty-two. But for now, prices are outrunning pay again.

lines.text: Subscribe for the week's biggest money story, explained on a whiteboard.
lines.say: If this helped, subscribe for the week's biggest money story, explained on a whiteboard.

post.title: Average pay rose 3%. Prices rose 3.7%. Inflation's comeback week, explained
post.ig: Average hourly pay rose 3%. Prices rose 3.7%. Here's what inflation's comeback means for your money.
post.tiktok: Pay up 3%, prices up 3.7%. Inflation's comeback, explained.
post.yt_desc:
Average hourly pay rose 3% in the year to September 2026, but prices rose 3.7%, so real hourly pay fell 0.7%. In two days in October, the consumer price index, producer prices (up 6.3% over a year), Freddie Mac's 7.4% mortgage rate and Social Security's 3.6% COLA all told the same story, with the Fed's next decision on Oct 28. This video compares 2026 with the 1970s and with 2021-22, and walks through what it means for paychecks, savings, debt and 401(k)s, with labeled examples.

Sources: BLS CPI and Real Earnings (Oct 14, 2026); BLS PPI (Oct 15, 2026); BLS Employment Situation (Oct 2, 2026); Social Security Administration (Oct 14, 2026); Freddie Mac (Oct 15, 2026); Federal Reserve (Sept 16, 2026); Census Bureau (Oct 15, 2026); FDIC national rates; Federal Reserve G.19; Bank of America and JPMorgan Q3 2026 results; Federal Reserve History; AP and Axios (Dec 2022); CNBC; CNN.

News and education, not financial advice.
